subcategory: san joaquin valley saltbush scrub shrub

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, lean sandy or loamy soil in full sun; seed germinates better with some soil cover since it responds poorly to light, and this slow-growing shrub needs a full season before it reads as an established plant.

directions: Cattle saltbush is a gray-green, densely branched shrub that dominates vast stretches of the San Joaquin Valley floor and Carrizo Plain saltbush scrub, often forming the only woody cover across alkaline clay flats too salty for most other shrubs. Its small, scurfy leaves and inconspicuous cream and yellow flowers give way to tiny bracted fruits that were historically browsed by livestock and wildlife across the valley's grazing lands. It demands fast-draining sandy or loamy ground and resents any clay that stays wet, declining quickly if irrigated beyond its natural rainfall pattern. Use it as an anchor shrub in a dry alkali-flat or valley-floor native planting rather than a conventional border, where its slow, long-lived habit rewards patience.

subcategory: california valley floor desert jointfir shrub

planting.note: Fall-sow into coarse, fast-draining sandy soil to allow natural winter stratification, or set out container stock in spring; give it room away from irrigated beds since overwatering young plants is the most common failure.

directions: California jointfir is a stiff, leafless-stemmed desert shrub scattered across the sandy and gravelly flats of the San Joaquin Valley and Carrizo Plain, where its jointed, blue-green stems photosynthesize in place of true leaves. Separate male and female plants produce small cone-like structures at the stem nodes in spring, and the dried stems have long been steeped into a mild, caffeine-free tea by both Native Californians and early settlers. It needs only coarse, fast-draining soil and full sun, tolerating extreme summer heat and long dry stretches once its deep root system is established. Avoid clay or any regularly irrigated bed, which leads to slow decline rather than vigorous growth.

subcategory: san joaquin valley floor annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, fast-draining sand or decomposed granite in full sun; this valley-floor annual needs open, undisturbed ground and does poorly if crowded by grass or mulch.

directions: Thistle sage is one of the showiest spring annuals of the Carrizo Plain and southern San Joaquin Valley floor, sending up a spiny, cobwebbed rosette of thistle-like silver-gray foliage topped by whorled clusters of fringed, lavender-blue flowers with conspicuous orange anthers. It is a true desert-adjacent sand and clay specialist, thriving only on bare, fast-draining ground in full sun and disappearing quickly if competing grasses or mulch crowd the seedlings. Large carpenter bees and other big-bodied native bees are its primary pollinators, making it a strong addition to a dry wildflower meadow built around valley-floor annuals. Let it dry down and shatter its own seed in place each summer for a self-sustaining stand the following spring.

subcategory: san joaquin valley floor grassland annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto clay or gravelly open ground in full sun; this valley grassland annual germinates with the first soaking fall rains and needs no irrigation beyond that.

directions: Great Valley phacelia is a short, bristly-stemmed annual of clay and gravelly grassland slopes across the San Joaquin Valley floor and surrounding foothills, producing loosely coiled clusters of lavender-blue, bell-shaped flowers in early spring that are an important early forage source for native bees. It grows readily among native bunchgrasses and other valley-floor annuals rather than needing a cleared bed of its own, filling bare patches in a dryland grassland planting. Direct sow onto undisturbed clay or gravelly soil in fall and let rainfall carry it through to spring bloom, since it does not tolerate summer irrigation or rich garden soil. Expect it to set seed and vanish by early summer like the rest of the valley's spring annual flora.

subcategory: san joaquin valley alkali scrub subshrub

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or set out container plants in spring on lean, mineral-rich alkali flat or gypsum soil in full sun; it needs no amendment and performs worse in enriched garden soil.

directions: Alkali goldenbush is a bushy, resinous subshrub that colonizes salty, mineral-rich alkali flats and gypsum soils across the San Joaquin Valley floor and Carrizo Plain where few other woody plants can persist. Clusters of small golden-yellow daisy flowers appear over an unusually long season spanning summer through fall, providing nectar after most other valley-floor natives have gone dormant for the year. It thrives on neglect in the leanest, saltiest soil available and needs essentially no supplemental water once established, declining instead when given rich soil or regular irrigation. Pair it with saltbush and other alkali-scrub natives for a low, long-blooming restoration or dry-garden planting on salty ground.

subcategory: san joaquin valley floor wash shrub

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into loose, sandy wash or disturbed valley-floor soil in full sun; no seed pretreatment is needed and seedlings establish fastest where drainage is fastest.

directions: Cheesebush (long known as Hymenoclea salsola before being folded into Ambrosia) is a fast-growing, airy-stemmed pioneer shrub of sandy washes and disturbed ground across the San Joaquin Valley floor, with thread-like gray-green foliage that gives the whole plant a hazy, see-through silhouette. Small spring flower heads mature into cottony, bristled seed clusters that catch the wind and carry the plant quickly onto fresh sand deposits after flood events. It tolerates the poorest, most nutrient-starved sandy soil and needs no irrigation once past its first season, making it useful as a quick-establishing filler or erosion-control shrub rather than a showy ornamental. Give it full sun and fast drainage and otherwise leave it alone.

subcategory: san joaquin valley inland alkali flat groundcover

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into sandy, saline, or alkaline soil in full sun; give it light summer moisture the first year to help the rhizomatous mat knit together.

directions: Alkali heath is a low, wiry, mat-forming perennial that spreads by rhizome across saline and alkaline flats, and although it is best known from coastal salt marsh edges, it also occurs inland around the alkali sinks and seasonally wet playa margins of the San Joaquin Valley and Carrizo Plain. Tiny pink to white flowers stud the fine, needle-like foliage over a long spring-through-fall season, and the dense mat it forms can knit together bare salty soil where turf and most groundcovers fail outright. It tolerates heavy clay and standing winter water as readily as dry summer alkali crust, needing only a little supplemental moisture the first year to spread fully. Use it as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover on salty valley-floor ground rather than ordinary garden soil.
